<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README content, Chaos Monkey is a chaos engineering tool that’s designed to randomly terminate service instances (virtual machines, containers, etc.) in production environments – and it’s deeply integrated with Spinnaker. This diagram should capture both the internal modular design of the chaosmonkey system and its integration with external systems (like Spinnaker and various cloud provider backends).

Below is how you can approach drawing a complete and accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Command/Entry Point: Start with the primary executable for Chaos Monkey. Notice the “cmd/chaosmonkey” directory with its main.go that acts as the launcher.
   • Core Modules and Domain Logic: Identify several key packages that encapsulate the tool’s behavior:
     - Configuration: The “config” package (with submodules like “config/param”) that handles the configuration files and behavior.
     - Scheduling and Eligibility: Directories like “schedule”, “schedstore”, “eligible”, “outage”, and “deploy” which together determine what instances are eligible for termination, when to schedule terminations, and how to log/deploy the chaos actions.
     - Integration with External Platforms: The “spinnaker” directory plays a crucial role in integrating with Spinnaker (Netflix’s continuous delivery platform). This module contains components for loading configurations, sending termination commands, and handling URLs.
     - Supporting Utilities: Other domain-centric packages such as “cal”, “clock”, “constrainer”, “decryptor”, “errorcounter”, “grp”, “tracker” support the core functionality (like time management, configuring termination “constraints”, error counting, and tracking state).
     - Deployment/Migration: The “deploy” and “migration” directories (including SQL schema files) hint at potential backend state persistence or deployment orchestration that might be required for certain operational workflows.
     - Testing and Mocks: Although not part of production flow, the “mock” directories and various test files indicate which modules are critical and should be highly testable.

2. Define the Relationships and Interactions:
   • Entry Point to Core Modules: The diagram should show that the chaosmonkey binary (from cmd/chaosmonkey) calls into the core command logic (in the “command” directory) which further invokes configuration parsing, scheduling, eligibility checks, and termination procedures.
   • Configuration and Parameterization: Show that the “config” package drives the behavior of modules by providing runtime parameters and (possibly) external configuration values.
   • Scheduling/Eligibility Workflow: Draw arrows from scheduling to “eligible” (logic that decides which instances can be terminated) and “outage” (which implements the termination logic). Emphasize that modules like “cal” and “clock” support time-based scheduling aspects as well.
   • Integration with Spinnaker: Clearly indicate an integration layer (the “spinnaker” package) that connects Chaos Monkey with the external Spinnaker system. Use directional arrows from the core termination logic to Spinnaker, indicating API requests or command dispatches.
   • Deployment/Database Interaction: If applicable, include a side block for migration and persistence (using modules found in “mysql” and “migration”) used for storing schedules or logs related to instance terminations.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • Modular/Layered Design: From the entry point to various domain modules, highlight that the system is divided into functional packages. Although packaged together in a monolithic binary, each directory represents a well-defined layer or component.
   • Integration with External Services: Stress the separation between internal logic (eligibility, scheduling) and external integrations (Spinnaker and cloud APIs).
   • Testing/Mocks: You may include a note or an auxiliary block representing the importance of testing, with mocks in a separate section – ensuring that each module can be unit tested, reinforcing decoupling.

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Use clear labels for each component:
       – “Command/CLI (cmd/chaosmonkey)”
       – “Configuration Manager (config/)”
       – “Scheduling Engine (schedule, schedstore)”
       – “Eligibility and Outage Logic (eligible, outage, deploy)”
       – “Spinnaker Integration (spinnaker/)”
       – “Utility Modules (cal, clock, constrainer, decryptor, errorcounter, tracker)”
   • Draw directional arrows indicating data flows or dependencies:
       – For example, have arrows pointing from the CLI to the configuration manager, from configuration to scheduling, and then from scheduling to eligibility and finally to the Spinnaker integration.
       – Use arrows to show that deployment may also interact with database migration/persistence layers.
   • Use color-coding or distinct shapes:
       – Differentiate between internal modules (e.g., rectangle shapes) and external systems like Spinnaker or cloud APIs (e.g., ellipses or differently colored shapes).
       – Consider a color scheme that groups related modules together (e.g., one color for scheduling-related components, another for configuration/integration).
   • Be detailed but succinct:
       – Do not overcomplicate, but capture enough granularity that another engineer can see the separation of concerns – from the CLI down to the integration with Spinnaker and even testing utilities.

5. Practical Steps for Drawing:
   • Start by placing the primary launcher (cmd/chaosmonkey) at the center or top.
   • Branch out to show the configuration and command handling flow (the “command” directory acts as the business logic layer).
   • From there, lay out the scheduling and eligibility modules, linking them with supporting utilities.
   • Show how the decision flows into termination actions that interact with the Spinnaker module and external cloud provider APIs.
   • Include side-notes for testing and migration components.
   • Optionally, include ancillary components like “docs” and “travis.yml” as supporting elements that indicate CI/CD or documentation workflows but focus mainly on the core architecture.

By following this detailed breakdown and highlighting the relationships between the components, your system design diagram will effectively communicate the architecture of Chaos Monkey and how each piece interacts both internally and with external systems. This approach caters perfectly to the full-stack nature of the project by clearly separating concerns and emphasizing the integration with Spinnaker while showcasing the robust modular design of the chaos engineering tool.
</explanation>
